## Q1
Which of the following have true value when the universe of discourse is all integers?

A. ∃n (2n = 3n)<br>
B. ∃n (n² &gt; n)<br>
C. ∀n (2n &gt; n)<br>
D. ∃n (n² = 2)<br>
E. ∀x∀y ∃z (xy = z)

## Q1 - Options
(A) B, C and E only
(B) A, B and E only
(C) A, B, C and D only
(D) B, C, D and E only

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q3

A is true at n = 0, and B is true, for example at n = 2. C fails at negative integers, D is false because √2 is not an integer, and E is true because the product of any two integers is an integer. Hence A, B and E are true.

## Q2
Match List-I with List-II.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. Commutative law<br>B. Distributive law<br>C. De Morgan law<br>D. Absorption law | I. P ∧ (Q ∨ R) ≡ (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R)<br>II. P ∧ (P ∨ Q) ≡ P<br>III. P ∧ Q ≡ Q ∧ P<br>IV. ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q |

## Q2 - Options
(A) A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
(B) A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III
(C) A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
(D) A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q31

Commutativity is P ∧ Q ≡ Q ∧ P (III). Distribution is P ∧ (Q ∨ R) ≡ (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R) (I), De Morgan's law is ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q (IV), and absorption is P ∧ (P ∨ Q) ≡ P (II). Thus the apparently similar formulas in I and II must not be swapped: I expands a conjunction while II removes a redundant disjunction.

## Q3
Match the equivalent propositions in List-I and List-II.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. P → (Q → P)<br>B. P → (Q ∨ R)<br>C. (P → Q) ∧ (R → Q)<br>D. ¬(P ⇔ Q) | I. (P ∨ Q) ∧ ¬(P ∧ Q)<br>II. (P ∨ R) → Q<br>III. (P → Q) ∨ (P → R)<br>IV. ¬P → (P → Q) |

## Q3 - Options
(A) A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I
(B) A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
(C) A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV
(D) A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q63

For A, Q → P is ¬Q ∨ P, so P → (Q → P) is ¬P ∨ ¬Q ∨ P, a tautology; IV is also a tautology. For B, P → (Q ∨ R) becomes ¬P ∨ Q ∨ R, exactly III. Applying (X→Q) = ¬X∨Q to C gives (¬P∨Q)∧(¬R∨Q) = ¬(P∨R)∨Q, which is II. Finally ¬(P⇔Q) is true exactly when one, but not both, of P and Q is true, which is I.

## Q4
Which of the following statements are true if the universe of discourse for all variables consists of all integers?

A. ∀n∃m(n² &lt; m)<br>
B. ∃n∃m(n + m = 4 ∧ n − m = 2)<br>
C. ∃n∃m(n² + m² = 5)<br>
D. ∃m∀n(m + n = 0)<br>
E. ∀m∃n(m + n = 0)

## Q4 - Options
(A) A, B & C Only
(B) A, B, C & D Only
(C) A, B, C & E Only
(D) B, C, E & D Only

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q6

Each statement must be checked on its own quantifier structure before combining them.

- **A.** True. For any integer n, choosing m = n² + 1 always makes n² &lt; m, since integers are unbounded above.
- **B.** True. Solving n + m = 4 and n − m = 2 together gives n = 3 and m = 1, both integers, so such a pair exists.
- **C.** True. Taking n = 1 and m = 2 gives 1² + 2² = 5, so such integers exist.
- **D.** False. This asks for one fixed m that satisfies m + n = 0 for every integer n, but no single m can be the negative of every n at once.
- **E.** True. This asks whether, for every m, some n makes m + n = 0, and n = −m always works because n is chosen after m is fixed.

D and E look similar but the quantifier order reverses their meaning. E lets n depend on m, so it is always satisfiable, while D forces one m to work for all n, which is impossible. A, B, C and E hold, so A, B, C & E Only is correct.

## Q5
Which of the following logical implications are tautologies?<br>
A. [~p ∧ (p ∨ q)] → q<br>
B. ~p → (p → q)<br>
C. [p ∧ (p → q)] → q<br>
D. ~(p → q) → q

## Q5 - Options
(A) A & B Only
(B) B & D Only
(C) A, B & C Only
(D) B, C & D Only

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q31

An implication is a tautology when it evaluates to true for every combination of truth values of its variables.

- **A. [~p ∧ (p ∨ q)] → q** — this is true in every row: whenever ~p ∧ (p ∨ q) is true, p must be false and q must be true to make p ∨ q true, so q is guaranteed. It is a tautology.
- **B. ~p → (p → q)** — whenever p is false, the consequent p → q is automatically true, and whenever p is true, the antecedent ~p is false, making the whole implication true either way. It is a tautology.
- **C. [p ∧ (p → q)] → q** — this is modus ponens, one of the most basic valid inference forms, and it holds in every row of its truth table. It is a tautology.
- **D. ~(p → q) → q** — taking p = true and q = false makes p → q false, so ~(p → q) is true, but q itself is false, giving a true antecedent and a false consequent. The implication is false in this case, so D is not a tautology.

Only A, B and C hold in every case, so the correct set is A, B & C Only.

## Q6

(A) P → ¬Q; P ∧ ¬Q; Q → ¬P; P → ¬Q
(B) P → Q; ¬P ∧ ¬Q; ¬Q → P; ¬P → ¬Q
(C) P → ¬Q; ¬P ∧ ¬Q; Q → ¬P; ¬P → ¬Q
(D) P → ¬Q; P ∧ ¬Q; Q → P; ¬P → ¬Q

## Q6 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q56

“Neither” means ¬P ∧ ¬Q. “Not intelligent is necessary for happy” makes happiness imply not intelligent, Q → ¬P. The first and fourth implications are P → ¬Q and ¬P → ¬Q respectively, so only option C has all four forms.

## Q11
Consider the following, where p and q are two statements.

A. ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q<br>
B. ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q<br>
C. p ∧ ¬p ≡ T<br>
D. ¬(p ⇒ q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q<br>
E. p ∨ q ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q

## Q11 - Options
(A) (A), (B) and (D) only
(B) (A), (C) and (D) only
(C) (C), (D) and (E) only
(D) (A), (B) and (C) only

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q47

By De Morgan’s laws ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q, so (A) and (B) hold. For (D), p ⇒ q is ¬p ∨ q, so ¬(p ⇒ q) ≡ ¬(¬p ∨ q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q — also true. (C) fails because p ∧ ¬p is a contradiction, not a tautology, and (E) fails on the row p = q = T. Only (A), (B) and (D) — option A.

## Q19
Consider universe of positive integers X = {1 ≤ n ≤ 8}, proposition P = "n is an even integer", Q = "(3 ≤ n ≤ 7) ∧ (n ≠ 6)". Then the truth set of P ↔ Q is

## Q19 - Options
(A) {1, 4}
(B) {2, 6}
(C) {3, 4, 5}
(D) {1}

## Q19 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q62

P(n) is true for even n, and Q(n) is true exactly when 3 ≤ n ≤ 7 and n ≠ 6. Checking every n from 1 to 8 for P(n) ↔ Q(n) (true whenever P and Q agree):

- n=1: P=F, Q=F (outside 3–7) → match, true
- n=2: P=T, Q=F → mismatch, false
- n=3: P=F, Q=T → mismatch, false
- n=4: P=T, Q=T → match, true
- n=5: P=F, Q=T → mismatch, false
- n=6: P=T, Q=F (excluded by n≠6) → mismatch, false
- n=7: P=F, Q=T → mismatch, false
- n=8: P=T, Q=F (outside 3–7) → mismatch, false

The biconditional is true only for n = 1 and n = 4, giving truth set {1, 4}.

- **A. {1, 4}** — correct, matches the case-by-case check above.
- **B. {2, 6}** — both n=2 and n=6 give a mismatch between P and Q, not a match.
- **C. {3, 4, 5}** — includes n=3 and n=5, where P and Q disagree.
- **D. {1}** — misses n=4, which also satisfies the biconditional.

## Q20
Which of the following is NOT logically equivalent to P → Q?

## Q20 - Options
(A) ~P ∨ Q
(B) ~Q → ~P
(C) ~(P ∧ ~Q)
(D) ~Q → P

## Q20 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Propositional & Predicate Logic
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q1

P → Q is logically equivalent to ~P ∨ Q, its contrapositive ~Q → ~P, and ~(P ∧ ~Q) by De Morgan's law applied to ~P ∨ Q.

- **A. ~P ∨ Q** — this is the standard disjunctive form of P → Q.
- **B. ~Q → ~P** — the contrapositive, always equivalent to the original conditional.
- **C. ~(P ∧ ~Q)** — De Morgan's law turns this into ~P ∨ Q, the same as option A.
- **D. ~Q → P** — correct, this is not equivalent. It simplifies to Q ∨ P, which is a different truth function from P → Q, since it is true even when P is false and Q is false is the only case it shares a false value with the original.
